candidates.title: Score memories by recency, importance and relevance instead of summarising everything
candidates.rule: When agent memory exceeds the context window, retrieve a top-k subset scored by a weighted sum of exponential recency decay, LLM-rated importance (1-10), and embedding cosine relevance to the current query, rather than compressing the whole history into one summary.
candidates.passage: Summarizing all of Isabella’s experiences to fit in the limited context window of the language model produces an uninformative response
candidates.finding: The three-signal retrieval scheme is described with concrete parameters (decay 0.995, all weights 1, min-max normalisation) and an illustrative contrast against summarisation, but the paper does not run a controlled comparison of retrieval scoring variants; the summarisation comparison is anecdotal. The recommendation extrapolates from that example plus the ablation showing memory access matters.
workloads: agent interview questions about memories and relationships
candidates.conditions: Memory objects are natural-language strings with creation and last-access timestamps; importance is generated once at memory-creation time by a prompt; top-ranked memories fill the remaining context window.
candidates.limitations: No ablation isolates recency vs importance vs relevance, and no tuning study; the summarisation baseline is a single anecdote. Retrieval failures persisted: agents gave incomplete or embellished answers (e.g. recalling party plans but not the invitation).
candidates.validation_test: On the same interview set, compare full-history summarisation, relevance-only retrieval, and the three-signal weighted score at equal prompt lengths, measuring accuracy against ground-truth memory logs rather than subjective believability.

candidates.title: Expect retrieval misses and embellishment; verify agent claims against the memory log
candidates.rule: Do not treat a memory-augmented LLM agent's confident statements as evidence it holds the underlying memory; audit affirmative claims against the stored memory stream, because agents retrieve partial memories and add unsupported details.
candidates.passage: Out of the 453 agent responses regarding their awareness of other agents, 1.3% (n=6) were found to be hallucinated.
candidates.finding: The authors verified each affirmative knowledge claim against the agent's memory stream and found a small but nonzero hallucination rate, plus qualitative cases of partial retrieval (Tom recalling party plans but doubting the party existed) and world-knowledge embellishment (Adam Smith 'authored Wealth of Nations').
workloads: post-hoc interviews about information diffusion and mutual acquaintance
candidates.conditions: Verification done manually by inspecting memory stream entries after a two-day simulation; rate measured only for the 'do you know of X' question family.
candidates.limitations: Single run, one model, short horizon; the 1.3% figure is specific to acquaintance questions and manual labelling, not a general hallucination rate. No automated verification method was proposed or evaluated.
candidates.validation_test: Instrument an agent harness to require a memory-ID citation for each factual claim and automatically check it, then measure how often claims lack support across tasks and models, comparing to the manual audit rate reported here.

reason: The paper runs a controlled ablation of memory retrieval, planning, and reflection within one sandbox LLM-agent setup, with human ranking of believability. This supports narrowly scoped rules about adding retrieval-based memory, periodic reflection, and hierarchical plans; secondary observations (plan decomposition fixing repeated actions, cost) are design arguments rather than measured comparisons, so they are flagged as inferred or scoped carefully.
